narrative:
The model determined that you have an 84% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students, signaled to the model a high likelihood of struggling with the bar. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you placed in the second decile while accepted students averaged the sixth decile. Finally, your LSAT score of 30, compared with an average of 37 among those who were admitted, provided additional weight in the same direction.

None of these features suggested you would pass. Together they created a clear picture for the model that the risk of bar failure was too high to approve admission.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a meaningfully higher score, combined with improving your academic performance if you continue your studies, would be the most direct ways to shift a future prediction in your favor. Consider targeted bar-preparation resources early, and explore schools or programs that place less weight on these exact metrics.
